claims.text: Simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature accelerates coupled degradation in multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloys.
Potential differences between phases cause galvanic corrosion in multi-phase eutectic or hypereutectic high-entropy alloys.
An unstable passive film forms on a eutectic high-entropy alloy at elevated temperature in a corrosive environment.
Elevated temperature destabilizes the passive film.
Elevated temperature exacerbates galvanic corrosion between the phases.
Wear disrupts or ruptures the surface oxide film.
Oxide-film rupture during friction leads to adhesive and abrasive wear.
Galvanic corrosion, passive-film instability, and wear-induced oxide disruption act synergistically rather than independently.
The proposed synergy is the primary cause of the accelerated coupled degradation.
Total degradation will increase relative to a room-temperature or single-mechanism baseline.
The wear rate will increase relative to the stated baseline.
The corrosion current will increase relative to the stated baseline.
A relevant elevated-temperature boundary is 500°C to 1000°C.
A 3.5 wt.% NaCl environment is a relevant corrosive boundary condition.
Sliding wear is the specified mechanical degradation mode.
The magnitude of degradation and the relative mechanism contributions depend on alloy composition, temperature, and corrosive environment.
An absence of a significant degradation difference between simultaneous elevated-temperature exposure and room-temperature or single-mechanism conditions would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The proposed 500–1000°C range is combined with a 3.5 wt.% NaCl corrosive environment without specifying pressure, physical state, or another means of maintaining an aqueous chloride environment at those temperatures.
